title: Unit economics of a reply-drafting assistant
prompt: Finance wants to know if our AI reply-drafting assistant for support pays off. Numbers: 40,000 tickets a month. The model costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Each ticket uses 3 model calls averaging 6,000 input and 800 output tokens. Our pilot shows 70% of drafts are usable after a 1-minute agent review; when a draft is unusable, the agent spends 9 minutes doing the ticket manually. Today a ticket takes 8 minutes of agent time, and agents cost $40 an hour fully loaded. Is it worth it, and what's the break-even?

criteria.text: Computes the cost per completed ticket including model cost, review time and the cost of unusable drafts, arriving at approximately $2.56 (any value from $2.50 to $2.62).
States the baseline cost per ticket as about $5.33 and the monthly net saving as roughly $111,000 (any value from $105,000 to $117,000), or the equivalent annual figure.
Gives a break-even success rate of approximately 24% (any value from 22% to 26%), or an equivalent statement of the success rate below which the assistant costs more than today.
Points out that human review and failure handling, not model tokens, dominate the cost (model cost is about $0.09 per ticket).
Shows how the result changes under different assumptions, such as a lower success rate or a different volume (a sensitivity analysis).
Names missing cost items or assumptions to validate, such as build or one-time costs, fixed monthly costs, or whether the 70% pilot result holds on a larger evaluation set.

checks.description: States a cost per completed ticket of about 2.56
